value.a:
Vignobles Levet Côte-Rôtie 2022 is $240, bin 34331, filed under France, Rhône, Red, Côte-Rôtie, and our young Côte-Rôtie from a family estate.

Côte-Rôtie, koht roh-TEE, is the roasted slope: steep terraces above the Rhône at Ampuis. The rules allow up to 20 percent Viognier, though most growers use little or none; the dark schist of the Côte Brune gives firmer wine, the Côte Blonde more perfume.

Levet, luh-VAY, is a small Ampuis family estate farming only Syrah on both hillsides. The list prints no cuvée name: this is the house blend of the family’s parcels, fermented with a large share of whole bunches and aged about two years in demi-muids and large casks, mostly old. 2022 was hot and dry with a small crop, and the wine is dark cherry, wild blackberry and spice, earthy and firm.

The other Levet lines: the 2022 magnum, bin 13231 at $490, is this wine in 1.5 liters; the 2023, bin 22711 at $250, is the next vintage; Les Journaries 2022, bin 21562 at $260 and in magnum at $540, is the estate’s cuvée largely from old vines in La Landonne, sold in Europe as Maestria.

value.a:
Asked: Is there Viognier in it?

Answer: The appellation allows up to 20 percent, fermented with the Syrah, but the estate’s importers describe its vines as all Syrah. For this bottle I will confirm with the sommelier.

Asked: What does whole bunch mean?

Answer: Much of the fruit goes into the vat on its stems, uncrushed. Growers who do it look for freshness, spice and a firmer frame.

Asked: Is it ready to drink?

Answer: It is young and firm. Forty-five minutes in a decanter opens it; the sommelier decides on the night.

value.a:
Peay Vineyards Scallop Shelf 2023 is Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir at $180, bin 16651, filed under United States, Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast & County, and our cool coast California Pinot Noir.

Peay, PAY, is a family estate near Annapolis on the far Sonoma Coast, about four miles from the Pacific. It makes all its estate Pinot Noir, then chooses barrels for three blends, each from several clones and blocks. Scallop Shelf is named for the scallop fossils found in the soil at planting; the winery calls it its floral, red fruited blend.

The label reads West Sonoma Coast, the appellation approved in 2022 inside the larger Sonoma Coast. 2023 was cool and late after a wet winter, and the wine is fresh: red and black cherry, jasmine tea and forest floor.

The other Peay lines: Pomarium 2023, bin 15181 at $180, is the estate blend the winery calls its muscle, firmer in build; Savoy Vineyard 2023, bin 145131 at $180, is bought fruit from Anderson Valley in Mendocino County, more forward young, though the list files it under Sonoma; Les Titans 2013, bin 153221 at $120, is the estate Syrah.

value.a:
Asked: Why is it called Scallop Shelf?

Answer: The winery found scallop fossils in the soil when it planted the vineyard; the name is the ground, not a seafood pairing.

Asked: Is it a single vineyard?

Answer: It is all from Peay’s one estate, but blended from several clones and blocks chosen by barrel, not a single block.

Asked: Is it like Kosta Browne?

Answer: Both are Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir. Peay grows four miles from the ocean and is fresher and more floral; the Kosta Browne is riper and plusher.

Ring it in by bin 16651 and read Scallop Shelf on the label against the order. The label says West Sonoma Coast where our list prints Sonoma Coast; that is the same wine. Peay’s Les Titans 2013 is a Syrah on another page, not a Pinot Noir. How the 2023 was fermented and how much new oak it saw are not confirmed here, so those are questions for the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

value.a: Present the bottle and say Peay Vineyards, Scallop Shelf, West Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir, 2023, PAY. Serve it at 55 to 60°F in a Burgundy bowl, a few minutes in the ice bucket if the room runs warm; no decanting. Pour a taste for the host, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Scallop Shelf: red cherry and tea from four miles off the Pacific.”
